speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Taxis and private hire cars (PHCs) are very much part of this vision and complement our bus and Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In many other cities, the introduction of PHC booking service operators has led to disruptions, strikes and protests by taxi drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Here in Singapore, the Government, operators and the driver associations have worked closely together to address the challenges that came about as a result of technological disruption and the emergence of new players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The regulatory framework has evolved gradually and smoothly, in partnership with our tripartite colleagues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, we enjoy a P2P sector that is able to meet the needs of commuters and drivers, as well as our broader transport objectives, while also allowing innovation to thrive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This healthy balance is only possible with responsible operators, sensible commuters and safe drivers and, in addition, the active involvement of our colleagues from the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Transport led by Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and his deputy, Mr Ang Hin Kee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Prior to the entry of the ride-hail platforms into Singapore in 2013, P2P services were primarily delivered by 28,000 taxis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Taxi drivers would mostly cruise around or queue at taxi stands to look for and pick up passengers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is in contrast to what we label "ride-hail trips", where the ride is booked in advance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Prior to 2013, this booking was usually done by a phone call or text message and accounted for only a small proportion of rides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Long wait times and a lack of available taxis, especially during peak hours, were common complaints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: With the convenience and popularity of ride-hail applications, commuters have benefited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The matching of demand and supply has also been enhanced through these ride-hail apps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As a result, commuters now enjoy shorter waiting times for both street-hail and ride-hail trips.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Dynamic fares have also allowed better matching of supply and demand, with higher prices during peak hours and also lower prices during off-peak hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This allows commuters to have a range of options at different price points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Commuters have also benefited as operators innovate to attract passengers through pricing strategies, trip incentives and value-added services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There are even specialised services to meet different commuter needs, from families with young children to commuters with pets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Street-hail services will continue to have an important role and LTA's data shows that commuters prefer street-hail services in areas with a higher concentration of commuters and taxis, such as central areas and around Changi.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Commuters also prefer street-hail services for shorter trips as it is more efficient to street-hail a taxi than to wait for a booked ride.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Almost all respondents in a recent Customer Satisfaction Survey were satisfied with P2P services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The increased efficiency of matching drivers with commuters has benefited drivers as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Drivers have a higher chance of finding commuters and can also reduce the amount of time spent cruising without a passenger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: All this demonstrates how market-driven innovation can benefit commuters and drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Members can easily appreciate that if there were to be excessive regulations, this may compromise the current environment and the current situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: But it is also important to understand that these benefits can also easily be lost if there is insufficient regulatory oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: For example, operators may compromise commuter and driver safety at the expense of profits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Operators might also try to compete by "locking in" drivers using exclusive contracts, which would affect market contestability which, in turn, harms commuters by increasing prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This Bill has benefited from extensive consultations with operators, drivers, the National Taxi Association, the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, members of the public and the GPC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Their feedback, suggestions and active involvement have improved this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The framework aims to protect the safety and interests of commuters and drivers, while facilitating an open and innovative P2P sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, LTA already regulates taxi operators under the Road Traffic Act (RTA), and third party taxi booking service providers under the Third Party Taxi Booking Service Providers Act (TPB Act).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Like taxi operators, PHC booking service operators have an equally important responsibility in ensuring commuter and driver safety in the course of their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill will give LTA the necessary regulatory levers to ensure that the PHC booking service operators discharge these responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: With this change, LTA will have regulatory oversight over all major P2P operators in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, LTA has one set of regulations for taxi operators, which generally provide a mix of street-hail and ride-hail services, and another set of regulations for TPB service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: However, street-hail and ride-hail services have different characteristics and need to be regulated differently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will ensure that our regulations are fit for purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This means that taxi operators will be required under our new regulatory framework to hold separate licences for their street-hail and ride-hail services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: PHC booking service operators and TPB service providers will be licensed as ride-hail service operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will also be able to issue different sub-classes of street-hail and ride-hail service licences, such as for operators offering different types of services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, we already regulate drivers through the Taxi Driver's Vocational Licence (TDVL) and Private Hire Car Driver's Vocational Licence (PDVL) process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We currently also regulate vehicles at the vehicle level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: What this Bill sets out to do is to regulate the operators by regulating them on the basis of the service they provide, not on who the operator is.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: First, our licensing regime focuses on the larger operators, given the wider impact they have on commuters and drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will also manage regulatory costs for smaller ride-hail service operators and will allow small, new and innovative services to emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, all taxi operators have a minimum fleet size requirement of 800 taxis to ensure that they can provide an adequate level of service to commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to impose basic safety regulations on them to ensure commuter safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: These operators must ensure that their drivers and vehicles are appropriately licensed and insured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will continue to have the powers to issue a suspension order under the Road Traffic Act to prohibit drivers from driving for these exempt ride-hail service operators if their participating drivers fail to meet this requirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will continue to safeguard commuter safety via the separate licensing of drivers and vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will be an offence for any person to provide street-hail or ride-hail services without a licence or an exemption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: A further fine of up to $500 will be imposed for each day that the offence continues after conviction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will also be an offence to drive for these illegal operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill has provisions for LTA to have regulatory oversight over the entire P2P sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This includes the ability to regulate new business models or P2P services involving new vehicle types.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will allow LTA to respond quickly and effectively to rapid technological and commercial trends in the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will extend today’s safety-related regulations for taxi operators to all licensed ride-hail service operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The need for enhanced safety measures is an area that industry stakeholders and members of the public agreed is of critical importance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill will give LTA the powers to set safety requirements on licensed operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will track the number of accidents and driver offences that occur when a driver carries out a trip for a particular operator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Operators whose drivers have committed too many accidents or offences can be penalised through regulatory sanctions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is to ensure that operators play their part to encourage safe driving behaviour and reduce driver offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Operators must also ensure that the vehicles used to provide P2P services are able to pass the requisite vehicle inspections and are roadworthy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This ensures that operators play their part to keep the vehicles they deploy well-maintained and serviceable, for the safety of commuters, drivers and other road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill also gives LTA powers to issue emergency directives to all P2P operators, including licence-exempt service operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: For example, LTA will be able to prohibit operators from using vehicle models which are found to be defective and, therefore, pose safety risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Thirdly, in regulating the P2P sector, we will keep the market open to support the development of innovative and accessible services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We have benefited from having an open P2P sector, with increased ride availability and improved service standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We should continue to allow market forces to drive service delivery and improvement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is because such arrangements make it difficult for new players to enter the market and naturally favour incumbent operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is detrimental to driver and commuter interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will, however, make an exception for operators who directly employ drivers, as full-time employment is inherently exclusive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In line with our vision for an inclusive transport sector, we will ensure that P2P services continue to remain accessible to all commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: For now, LTA will continue to require taxi companies to provide call booking services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This ensures that those who may not be comfortable with an online booking process or an app, will continue to be able to book trips using a phone call.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: However, there are no such regulations for PHC fares.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Fare evasion and overcharging for PHC trips are also not prohibited, unlike for taxi trips today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The amendments will empower PTC to safeguard commuter and driver interests in the area of taxi and PHC fare transparency in the following ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Street-hail service operators will continue to be required to charge metered fares for street-hail taxi trips, in accordance with the fare structure now set by PTC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This allows commuters to compare fares across taxi operators more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Licensed ride-hail service operators will also be allowed to independently set flat fares for ride-hail trips using taxis and PHCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The only requirement is that these flat fares for taxi and PHC bookings by licensed ride-hail service operators must be provided upfront to commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will allow licensed operators to adjust both metered and flat fares.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is to deter such behaviour, to protect commuters and to protect drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will help to facilitate an open market to support the development of responsive P2P services, while also providing sufficient regulatory oversight to protect the safety and interests of commuters and drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It is a necessary piece in our long-term vision for a well-connected and convenient land transport network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This feedback has allowed us to better understand commuter, driver and industry needs and has helped to shape a better Point-to-Point Passenger Transport Industry Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Six years ago, Grab and Uber have disrupted our local taxi market.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At that time, taxi drivers were worried about livelihood.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They did not know whether they would be ousted.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison, taxi drivers and operators from other countries were also thinking of ways to stop PHCs from sinking roots into their local markets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some taxi drivers even had conflict with PHC drivers or went protesting on the streets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They did not think of a space where the two can co-exist.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compared to them, although our taxi drivers were also concerned, they did not create conflict and disturb our social order.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone has made huge effort, learn to adapt and use technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can cherish what we have today.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today we can discuss in a very peaceful environment to debate on this P2P legislation, we must thank our taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are very patient and adapt to market changes and challenges in a calm manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They believe we can provide a good arrangement for them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In many industries, new technologies, funds worth of billions of dollars and the digital economy have brought about many new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To be successful, the mindset of workers is more important.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our taxi drivers have demonstrated resilience by overcoming the challenges, embracing new things and learning to take on technologies as opposed to fearing them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, we also have taxi drivers in the gallery.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that in the subsequent debate today, we can give them a very positive response and give them some encouragement.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the first ride-hail operator I met was about six years ago in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Subsequently, many came and left, even as I participated in many debates about its impact.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, many livelihoods and commuter convenience are dependent on how the industry operates and how the LTA regulates the sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once this regulation of point-to-point is in place, I hope it will lead to fair competition among the various types of point-to-point operators and ensure greater accountability to our drivers and commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Back when Uber suddenly left Singapore a year plus ago, many felt that the way that these ride-hailing firms operate made it very easy for them to exit and it also left drivers, commuters and their employees in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nobody knew what happened because, overnight, they closed their office and all the senior management exited Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To avoid such negative outcomes, all street-hailing service and ride-hailing service operators should comply with the Tripartite Standards in managing self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In some cities, Mr Speaker, regulators have considered treating these drivers as employees because, truth be told, many of them are tied to employee-like requirements.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I believe Singapore, again, has a better solution in that the Tripartite Standards set forth by the Ministry of Manpower is a better option.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, many operators continue to unilaterally suspend drivers or offer contracts that say more about the obligations of drivers than what the obligations of the operators are.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, fair and reasonable terms should be the norm of contracts moving forward.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, our operators have also supported good schemes.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is the Enhanced Drive and Save MediSave co-contribution scheme offered by taxi operators, together with the National Taxi Association, for taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also the free insurance offered by Grab and Gojek with the National Private Hire Vehicle Association to help drivers manage loss of income due to prolonged illness.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are good measures and show that our operators are, indeed, responsible ones.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will not create new burdens on the existing operators because they are already currently doing many of these good things.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we also want to ensure that new operators coming to Singapore in future comply with the same type of good practices.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, to qualify as a private hire driver, you only need to have two years of driving experience.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, technically, at age 20, you can be a private hire driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison, to drive a taxi you need to be at least 30 years old and above.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The argument that ride hailing caters to part-timers and those who avail their vehicles in a sharing economy do not quite reflect reality.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, we have seen a surge in bidding of new cars by leasing companies and many drivers becoming full-time vocational drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we really want to see more young drivers doing this on a full-time basis, forgoing the opportunity to delve into a career, enlarging their skillsets and going professional in the work they do or to take a low-entry barrier job like vocational drivers?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, we have 20,000 taxis, 45,000 PHCs, plus 140,000 vocational drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The demand for such rides has slowed down since the exit of Uber.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recommend that all new applicants for PDVL to be similar as taxis and that they all be at least 30 years old and above and for Singaporeans only.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will disallow operators to prevent their drivers from taking jobs from others and reduce the risks of market domination by the operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that LTA has supported our call for this change.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One last point with regard to operators is the carpool platform.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are subjected to two trips a day where the driver is either on the way to work, to the market or somewhere else and he gives somebody a ride in exchange for a small fee to cover fuel or Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the feedback we have heard from taxi drivers as well as private hire drivers that there is this potential loophole.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If left unchecked, it would offer a backdoor to those who not want to comply with the operator or driver licensing requirements.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With appropriate regulatory oversight, Mr Speaker, I hope we will be able to attract more new point-to-point operators to our local scene, drive new innovations to bring about a better commuting experience for commuters and offer a sustainable career for drivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In times where speed, comfort, convenience or connectivity are desired, such point-to-point transportation helps to fill in the gaps that our rail and bus infrastructure may not be able to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the industry was not always able to bridge that gap and has led to ride-hailing, working on the principles of the sharing economy, to disrupt the market.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, all disruptions to the market, given time, will become part of the new normal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ride-hail, while bringing much-needed competition and innovation to the P2P transport space, has been regulated initially as a technology disruption, rather than a transportation alternative.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the Bill, but I do have concerns surrounding the P2P transport landscape that I wish the Senior Minister of State can give clarity to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since then, it has had to operate under the terms set forth by the CCCS judgment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the CCCS judgment hinged on defining the provision of ride-hailing platforms and crucially excluded street-hail providers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOT and LTA should ensure that the constraints currently on Grab do not just loosen overnight as the potential for abusing its market position is still there.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What measures will the Government be taking to prevent this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is not clear in the Bill whether the regulation of such fares and its related standards will be determined.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, any fare regime must balance the needs of allowing drivers to earn a meaningful living, while the commuters themselves do not need to pay exorbitant prices, especially during peak hours and times of stress in our public transport infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This potentially includes, among others, the matters on the condition of vehicles, conduct of drivers, and measures to deal with customer complaints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it may be reasonable to expect street-hail operators to follow existing taxi regulations, it is not clear how such Codes of Practices will look like for ride-hail operators.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister of State will provide some clarity to the House on this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the meantime, I would like to touch on three topics related to P2P transport that I hope the Senior Minister of State can clarify on how they will tackle in the industry moving forward.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research by researchers from the University of Chicago and Rice University on US transport cases has shown that the arrival of ride-hailing services has led to an increase in motor vehicle and fatal accidents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Preliminary data in Singapore from motor insurers indicate an increase in road accident rates since the debut of ride-hailing firms.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State whether the Government is satisfied with the overall quality of PHC drivers in respect of safe driving, knowledge competency, driving skills and considerateness while driving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Senior Minister of State think that more can be done to improve the standards in these respects?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State what measures will be taken to mitigate against the continuing risk of more accidents arising from PHCs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, a related issue or concern is that of child seats.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as taxis do not need to carry child seats currently, PHCs do need to have child seats for use when they have young children as passengers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the consultation phase of these regulations, more than half support having child seats in all P2P vehicles, including taxis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I can appreciate that there may not be easy answers for the Government, there has to be some consistency in its policymaking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If child seats are deemed to be a safety necessity for children travelling in PHCs, young children travelling in taxis without child seats are surely subject to the same hazardous risks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other parts of the world, Uber drivers have gone on strike demanding better pay at the same time Uber went public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as companies here seem to be able to give drivers meaningful income, only the ride-hailing operators are clear whether their drivers are able to earn a liveable income while driving reasonable hours so as not to result in tired drivers, endangering the lives of commuters and the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Crucially, drivers should also be able to earn a liveable and meaningful wage driving for ride-hail operators but with reasonable working hours.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government have any comparative statistics of the average working hours and average income of our PHC drivers vis-à-vis their counterparts in other first-world cities?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, are both the average hours they work each day as well as their daily income comparable with those of their counterparts in other first-world cities?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the incentives set by the operators causing drivers to work an unhealthy number of hours, for example, more than eight or 10 hours?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if so, should we be concerned with the impact on the drivers' health and families?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would this issue be regulated in the Code of Practices or other regulations?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the proposed code of practices will be specifying a time limit for video and audio recordings to be deleted so that the privacy of individuals can be safeguarded and what will such time limits be?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, there may also be a need to assess whether too many young adults may be lured by the promise of flexibility and wages they can gain from PHC driving as opposed to finding other employment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Senior Minister of State have the data for PHC drivers broken down by age?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concern here is that, career training-wise, such young adult drivers, particularly those who do private hire driving as a full-time occupation, may risk becoming obsolete with the possible advent of autonomous vehicles in perhaps the not-too-distant future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, younger PHC drivers may find themselves unemployable earlier in their working life and would need to retrain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government may really need to encourage more pathways to skill up PHC drivers as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also want to speak on the impact that the operator-owned or -run PHCs has on the value of Certificate of Entitlement (COE) premiums.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the departure of Uber, we saw the sharp drop in COE prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With Gojek entering the market, the COE prices have picked up again earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be fair, such big players buying or leasing a big fleet of cars having a distortionary effect on the value of COE premiums is not new to PHCs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Taxi operators were once bidding for COEs and they, too, had an undesirable impact on the COE prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For our stated zero-car growth policy, having idle cars is a market failure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is also all rather unfair to individual car owners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There has also been media reports of news or speculation that taxi companies may be allowed to bid for COEs again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I seriously hope that the Government is not entertaining this thought.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will certainly lead to an unwelcome spike in COE prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Alternatively, LTA should limit the fleet size of taxi and PHCs and ensure that all P2P passenger transport operators are not able to bid for COEs with other passenger cars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, although I support this Bill, I do have a few reservations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, in respect of our full-time PHC drivers, I would like to ask the Minister whether the average working hours each day as well as their daily income are comparable with those of their counterparts in other first-world cities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the incentives set by the operators causing drivers to work an unhealthy number of hours, for example, more than eight hours?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if so, should we be concerned with the impact on the driver's health and families?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from this, can the drivers' income be guaranteed?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to know whether these concerns that I have mentioned above would be regulated in the Code of Practices or other regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A few years ago, when the ride-hailing service was introduced in Singapore, Uber and Grab entered the market and COE prices saw an upsurge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the subsequent few years, COE prices continued to rise significantly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the departure of Uber, COE prices fell sharply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When Gojek entered the ride-hailing market this year, COE prices rose once again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such price fluctuations are not welcomed by private car owners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would like the Government to consider the following suggestions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, we should set up a different COE category for the ride-hailing companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, we should limit the number of cars that can be owned by them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, we can consider not allowing the ride-hailing operators to directly bid for COEs with owners of other private cars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): I look forward to the Senior Minister of State’s clarifications.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Six years after the first ride-hailing company entered Singapore, MOT has finally decided to regulate the ride-hailing sector more comprehensively.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is late but it is better to be late than never.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One taxi company, SMART Taxi, exited the market in 2013, the same year Grab entered Singapore to grab a share of the P2P market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: China started to regulate the PHC sector comprehensively in 2016, almost three years earlier than us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the same year, 2016, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development also published a paper on the regulation pertaining to the for-hire passenger transport.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: China's regulations have stipulated clearly that they would like to have the co-existence of taxis and PHCs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In London, licensed taxis decreased by a mere 1,000 from 2013 to 2017, while PHCs increased from 50,000 to 87,000, a 74% increase.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When we compare Singapore's situation with that of China and London, the contrast is significant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State if MOT has a view on the right mix of the number of registered taxis and PHCs, or is MOT happy to allow market forces to determine the equilibrium mix of taxis and PHCs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In determining the policy intention and direction, I would like to point out that there is a severe market imperfection in the P2P passenger transportation industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is one of the reasons why CCCS is still not removing the restrictions on the large ride-hail company.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the regulation of fare, Mr Speaker, Sir, earlier this year, Indonesia announced that it would regulate ride-hail fare, with a maximum and minimum fare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Very often, ride-hail passengers are irritated by surge pricing where the fare can surge by 100%, 200% or more whenever there is a shortage of vehicles or there is a sudden surge of demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State whether the P2P Bill that proposes to impose a ride-hail fare pricing policy is a signal that the authority is ready to regulate ride-hail fare or is it a mere provision to regulate the ride-hail fare in the future that is far, far away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the qualification of drivers, both taxi and PHC drivers send passengers from point A to point B.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Yet, it is easier to be a PHC driver than a taxi driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does MOT have the intention to enlarge the supply of PHC drivers and shrink the supply of taxi drivers?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: PHC drivers can be either a Singaporean or Permanent Resident (PR), although PR needs to work as a chauffeured-service driver.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There is a historical reason why taxi drivers need to be 30 and above.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I suppose the same logic applies to PHC drivers unless MOT thinks that the PHC drivers are a totally different category as compared to taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We note that under clause 30, LTA is empowered to issue one or more codes of practice to street-hail and ride-hail operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, taxi companies – or in the future, renamed as street-hail operators – have to provide trip data to LTA in real time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If so, the real-time trip data would enable LTA to better analyse the overall travel pattern of all passengers using P2P transport providers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such real-time data can also assist LTA and users of P2P services in the following ways.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One, when a passenger loses an item in a bookable vehicle, as defined in clause 4 of the Bill, LTA can help to locate the lost item in the PHC or taxi in real time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This piece of work is best undertaken by LTA, as a bookable vehicle is able to take booking jobs from different ride-hailing platforms and different operators within a single day or even within a single hour.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Two, LTA can better identify the appropriate ride-hail operator when the driver has committed an offence or met with an accident.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the sandbox regulation, under clause 5b, it is stated that one of the purposes of the Bill is to enable development and operation of innovative and accessible P2P passenger transport services which contribute to the mobility and safety of people in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, it is understandable that clauses 24 to 26 under Part 4 of the Bill allow LTA to exempt a ride-hail operator from applying for a licence, especially if it is an aggregator of a few ride-hail services like what Google is doing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand these clauses are meant to encourage innovation and thus the provision of a sandbox regulation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I notice that a similar provision for sandbox regulation is not provided under Part 3 of the Bill for street-hail services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does MOT think that street-hail services cannot innovate?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have a case in hand whereby a startup named "Vouch" would like to refer taxi services provided by existing taxi operators to hotel concierge through a chatbot.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Such a service is similar to that provided by Google where it aggregates ride-hail services from a few ride-hail operators and Google is exempted from applying for a ride-hail licence under sandbox regulation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Apparently, the said startup Vouch is required to apply for a third-party taxi licence but not Google.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many passengers choose to pay the ride-hail fare by cashless mode, especially by way of credit or debit card.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Attempts by the ride-hail operators to recover the fare often drew a blank.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If so, it will serve as a strong deterrent to those who want to cheat the fare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, taxi drivers have been troubled by PHCs for many years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The PHCs are, essentially, pirate taxis in disguise when they first entered the market.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They are unrestrained and not regulated by LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is unwise and risky not to regulate PHCs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This Bill comes late but it is better late than never.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have been a Member of Parliament for more than eight years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many residents, including taxi drivers, approach me to appeal for waiver of their traffic offences.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, many residents have also told me that PHC drivers often use their fingers to fiddle with global positioning system (GPS) on their phones while driving.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, they often make sudden turns in order to follow GPS instructions, endangering themselves, passengers and other road users.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that this Bill will allow LTA to have better oversight over PHC's safety and the safety of passengers and other road users.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is also essential for LTA to treat taxi drivers and PHC drivers equally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When I read Parts 4 and 5 of the Bill, I discover that MOT seems to be imposing the current regulations governing taxi operators on ride-hail service operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the surface, LTA appears to level the playing field.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, clause 30(2)(i) stipulates the Quality of Service that taxi operators have to meet.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, clause 30 2(i) also requires ride-hail service operators to meet a set of service standards.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When pressed by the operators, LTA appears to have no intention to require the ride-hail service PHC operators to meet the same service standards as the street-hail service taxi operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: PHC passengers are often annoyed by the surge pricing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that LTA can do something about this.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, I would like to appeal to MOT to spell out clearly what are the regulations that will be implemented in the near future, and what are the clauses in the Bill that are mere provisions to be implemented much later or during an emergency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, the Bill may give the impression that it is more form than substance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Taxi drivers have been serving Singaporeans and Singapore for the past 54 years since our Independence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When this Bill becomes an Act, I hope that taxi drivers will continue to survive, continue to serve our nation, and will not be diminished to a mere historical figure.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the P2P Passenger Transport Industry Bill is an important step to regulate the ride-hail industry which has grown very big.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While I support the Bill, I hope MOT can help to address the above irregularities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.03 pm until 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: And I have a clarification I would like to seek from Mr Dennis Tan on his comment in Mandarin, if I may.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: (In Mandarin):   Earlier on, Mr Dennis Tan mentioned that in terms of the working hours and the salary of the drivers, that that is his concern.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, I am just wondering whether he is equally concerned about the working hours and the income of our taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: And is the Member proposing to limit the working hours of the drivers or to increase the fare, in other words, is he looking at increasing the taxi fares so that the taxi drivers will enjoy higher incomes or is he proposing to our operators to cut down the fuel charge or to cut down the ERP fares in order to allow our taxi drivers to enjoy higher incomes without reducing their working hours?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My concern would be the same for whether it is the taxi drivers or the PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is a concern that I have for the industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Sorry, I shall, therefore, revert to English since the reply is in English.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The point I was trying to make was, yes, we are all concerned about the hours you put on the road and the pressure you face on the road.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The issue then is: do you, therefore, seek to ask that we reduce the hours and, therefore, you want to balance the cost by reducing the car rental or by increasing the fees that the commuters pay for each ride they take so that the drivers need not work such long hours on the road?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am raising the issue for the Senior Minister of State to discuss with the industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, I am not making a proposal as such.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I welcome this new Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should welcome more industry players to the industry and offer incentives to both drivers and customers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should take note that the operators have provided incentives to encourage drivers to attend to commuters' need during non-peak hours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has any customer satisfaction survey been done for different age groups and different types of customers, such as those who are information technology (IT)-savvy and those who are not?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure passengers welcome these new regulations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Bear in mind that we need to balance the conflicting needs between drivers who hope for higher incomes and customers who hope for lower fares.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I propose that a new definition of the private chauffeur services be provided within the new framework in order to clearly distinguish it from the ride-hail services.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Government also have the number of drivers working for each operator and the number of drivers who work in each band, for example, 24 to 30 hours, 31 to 40 hours, 41 to 50 hours and so forth?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Ministry will consider the suggestions I have just made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the whole, the provisions of this Bill are a step in the right direction and I do not oppose it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This kind of market concentration is unhealthy and would allow the vendor to have an unusually high degree of bargaining power vis-à-vis both commuters and drivers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand other players are present and ramping up, such as Gojek, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government provide an update on two questions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CCCS infringement decision about the Grab-Uber case from 2018 stated "CCCS has examined internal documents of the parties and found that Uber would not have left the Singapore market by simply terminating its business if the transaction had not taken place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, Uber would have continued its operations in Singapore while exploring other strategic commercial options, such as collaboration with another market player or a sale to an alternative buyer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The transaction has removed Grab's closest competitor and ride-hailing platform services, namely, Uber.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CCCS has received numerous complaints from both riders and drivers on the increase in effective fares and commissions by Grab post-transaction." In 2018, I filed a Parliamentary Question on the matter of relative merits of a mandatory notification regime for M&A deals which is practised in the European Union (EU), US, Vietnam and the Philippines for deals above certain specified thresholds, versus Singapore's current voluntary notification regime where some variant is practised in the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As part of his reply, at that time, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Dr Tan Wu Meng said, "On the other hand, under a mandatory notification regime, all merging parties that cross predetermined notification thresholds have to notify the Competition authority regardless of whether there are competition issues or not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This imposes compliance costs in businesses and may impede common place market activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also requires larger commitment on the Competition authority's resources to ensure that all mergers that cross the notification thresholds are duly notified, and to review these mergers." I acknowledge that this discussion touches on general competition policy rather than the P2P per se, but in the context of this Bill and in the light of what happened when Uber sold its assets to Grab in 2018, I would nonetheless like to ask if there will be consideration of measures to prevent a recurrence of a similar outcome.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Major market changing M&A deals do not occur all the time and huge changes in market share are not necessarily extremely difficult to measure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Compliance costs related to pre-approving major M&A deals may not be unduly high on the part of either the business sector or the regulator.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A mandatory approval regime does not appear to have deterred M&A transactions in the US and the EU.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One could argue that dynamic pricing can address all needs, as those with greater price sensitivity can wait for the dynamic prices to fall.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, a fixed price option provides greater assurance and peace of mind to those who really need it, even if it is associated with longer wait times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, my colleague Mr Dennis Tan spoke about the future advent of autonomous vehicles and how this might lead to the obsolescence of the skills acquired by P2P transport drivers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government given some thought to this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government consider working closely with the driver community such that when autonomous vehicles are about to be phased in, drivers are notified ahead of time and given some runway and facilitation to reskill and move to a different industry if they choose to do so?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Taxis were debated on 750 separate occasions since the Legislative Assembly first sat in 1955.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A basic question, which we are debating today, is whether and to what extent taxi services should be subject to regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the early years after Independence, the poor quality of our public bus services, combined with restrictions on the number of taxis, led to huge demand for pirate taxis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When the White Paper on the Reorganisation of Motor Transport Service of Singapore was tabled in 1970, there were only 3,800 licensed taxi cabs, but an estimated 7,000 or more pirate taxis in service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question then was: what to do with them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Yong Nyuk Lin, then Minister for Communications, stated in Parliament on 9 April 1969, and I quote: "I agree that pirate taxis, though running illegally, are performing a form of social function in providing an element of public transport service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But they are performing this function at the expense of the law-abiding licensed taxis and the bus companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They are able to operate at a much lower cost because they pay less tax, incur very little maintenance expenditure and pay no insurance cover for passenger liability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, they offer an unhealthy type of competition to the licensed operators which is harmful to our long-term planning for an improved public transport service in Singapore." Sir, the basic regulatory questions are the same then as now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The 1970 White Paper put an end to pirate taxis, added thousands of licensed taxi cabs and helped create the Worker’s Transport Co-operative, the forerunner of Comfort Taxi.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The recent changes to our taxi industry have been just as dramatic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have had a two-fold increase in P2P hire vehicles in just a few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Commuters complained in the early 2010s about the quality and availability of taxi services, especially during peak hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There was pent-up demand for P2P transport that was not being met by the incumbent taxi industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Private hire platforms, such as Grab and Uber, stepped in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, they provided third-party booking services for taxis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Then, they introduced private hire rides, which were quickly embraced by Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What led to such disruptive change in our P2P transport systems?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should acknowledge that these private hire platforms used investor financing to operate at a loss to grow rapidly, subsidising cars, drivers and commuters alike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the problem of unmet demand for P2P transport was caused, at least in part, by regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For decades, our taxi services have been subject to strict regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a bad thing by itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Visitors to Singapore are impressed by our high quality, clean and safe taxi cabs who strictly charge by the meter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans who travel know that in some other cities, you are putting your life and wallet at risk when taking taxis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But a long era under regulation often leads to excessive caution and perhaps even complacency, by both the regulator and the regulated industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Under regulation, our taxi services were not able to meet demand because they did not increase fleet size rapidly enough, did not address difficulties in booking taxis and did not innovate in fares and service offerings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not fair for me to speculate on whether responsibility lies at the feet of regulators, versus the regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it is clear that P2P transport regulation must have a holistic objective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I commend this Bill for specifying in the primary legislation that regulation should achieve not just the traditional goals of quality, safety and reliability, but also efficiency, innovation, social impact and sustainability, as part of the broader urban transport system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think reasonable people will agree with these broad objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question lies in what these objectives mean in practice and what regulators will do with the considerable powers afforded by this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Regulators will have the power to control fares, vehicle and driver quantity, driver contracting, quality of service and licence ownership – in short, nearly all substantive aspects of the P2P system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It mandates that P2P firms provide the Government with unprecedented access to data on key competitive aspects, including ride data, prices charged and, potentially, the algorithms that determine fares and matching.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope the Ministry will discuss in detail the objectives of regulatory policy and how they shall be measured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Clarity is especially important because these regulations, when enforced, will affect not only all commuters, but the livelihoods of tens of thousands of drivers, and billions of dollars of investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This seems to be difficult to enforce without a policy statement setting out what is, in fact, "adequate and satisfactory" and what are the specific benchmarks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is how to trade off efficiency and equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A completely efficient system may not be fair, and a completely fair system may be slow, unreliable and costly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The network economies of P2P ride-hailing platforms, and the use of advanced pricing algorithms based on big data, inherently generate this tradeoff or, at least, they create substantial risks that efficiency gains will be exploited by platforms at the expense of other stakeholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before I touch on efficiency, let me first touch on equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think most commuters in Singapore will wonder what is so unfair about taxi and ride-hailing services, grumbles about surge pricing aside.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But that is because we enforce certain basic principles of service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we enforce the cab-rank rule: commuters and taxis must be served in the order they start queuing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We enforce universal service: for-hire drivers cannot refuse to take a passenger to their destination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These are not principles unique to Singapore, but I daresay we are better than most in enforcing them for the benefit of all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Those who want to fly and who can pay more, get their seats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Airlines respond to profit by scheduling more or fewer flights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But airline tickets are often priced and sold in ways that can seem unfair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The same flight from A to B costs a different amount depending on when you bought it, which connection you are taking, whether you are a frequent flyer or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some price differences are justified by differences in costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Airlines do their best to charge different customers the most they can, for exactly the same service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These pricing principles can be readily applied to P2P markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A ride-hailing provider can prioritise favoured commuters and give them shorter wait times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A commuter who is price-sensitive could be given larger discounts, which means that less price-sensitive commuters pay higher fares.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fares today treat each trip in isolation, but trips are part of a network.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An efficient fare might mean that you should pay more if your driver has to reposition after completing your trip.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, let me touch on efficiency, which is less straightforward than it seems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Efficiency, in a narrow sense, means satisfying transport demand using as few real resources – cars, drivers, time and money – as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the broader sense, efficiency means integrating P2P travel into the public transport network so that our overall demand for urban travel is satisfied at the least cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is often mistaken for efficiency, but is in fact not efficiency?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Low prices, unfortunately, are not a direct gauge of efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A P2P trip can be very cheap but inefficient if it discourages commuters from taking the MRT which parallels the route.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A low price is not efficient if it is subsidised, or if it is because regulations on public safety are being evaded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nor is quantity or availability a measure of efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Commuters enjoy having a full taxi rank, or short booking times, but this is hardly efficient if taxis are sitting idle at the taxi stand, or if many drivers are cruising empty looking for fares.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One central reason why there is a tradeoff between efficiency and equity is that ride-hailing platforms have network economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The larger they get, the more commuters and drivers they have, the more efficient they become, because the chance of finding a good match goes up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But of course, when they are large, they also have more market power over both commuters and drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But they also show that if the market is segmented between street-hail and ride-hail, then outcomes are negative – wait times go up, trips go down.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These studies show that network size, which is achieved through market concentration, leads to efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that a large ride-hailing platform is efficient but has inherent market power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While commuters may grumble about high prices, they are willing to pay if they can get fast and reliable P2P services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In "Using Big Data to Estimate Consumer Surplus: The Case of Uber", published as a National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) working paper in 2016, Cohen et al find that commuters on Uber are very price inelastic – they still book rides even when surge prices rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An 8% increase in fares, for example, only leads to a 3% reduction in bookings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is important because it suggests ride-hailing platforms have considerable room to raise prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The ability of a large platform to raise prices has already been demonstrated at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As more of our P2P network gets converted to ride-hailing, our street-hailing network becomes less dense and, hence, less efficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think our regulatory policy cannot ignore these economic principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A policy should be developed that aims to maximise the efficiency benefits of P2P transport services while protecting commuters and drivers against the market power of these platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few suggestions for policy principles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The standards of service and quality across street-hail and ride-hail licensees should be harmonised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Segmentation of these markets along any dimension is likely to lessen the intensity of competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One issue concerns child seats, which are required in PHCs but not in taxis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Harmonisation that aims for a common high standard of safety will ensure that the relevant market and the intensity of competition will be as high as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The same harmonisation process should apply to how prices and quantity are regulated, with the aim of allowing both street hail and ride-hailing licensees to enjoy maximum flexibility subject only to restrictions to protect the public interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Under this Bill, taxis will continue to face restrictions on fleet size that PHCs are not subject to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When combined with the fact that taxis cannot be readily converted to non-taxi use, this means that taxi fleets are inherently less adaptable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, ride-hailing licensees are also subject to regulation on the quantity of drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that having a driver on your platform does not equal having a driver available for service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second principle I suggest is to develop a stated policy for guiding the industry to maximise the efficiency benefits of network size, while minimising the potential for abuse of market power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Every major platform aims to maximise the size of their driver and commuter network while creating barriers to entry for competitors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To counteract this, drivers and commuters must face minimal or no barriers to switching among platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government already aims to eliminate driver exclusivity contracts, we should consider if it is possible to go further, by facilitating multi-homing, that is, having drivers and commuters match through many platforms at once, rather than one platform at a time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is possible that the efficiency benefits of network size are so large that we will end up with a monopoly or dominant platform facing little competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The presumption is that the dominant ride-hailing platforms will continue to be well-organised and identifiable, allowing for regulatory levers to shape behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there are innovations that blur the line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are decentralised booking systems, such as those based on blockchain, or those which run through social networks or messaging apps, that do not fall neatly within the ambit of this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are services which claim not to operate for profit, such as social car pooling, and which thus appear to fall outside the ambit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And there are third parties linked to the industry, such as PHC rental companies, which appear to fall outside the ambit if they are nominally independent of the platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not expect that we will be able to answer all these questions today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But these are issues that our regulators will have to grapple with in the years ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But while this legislation is comprehensive, the real test lies in how LTA will use these powers to wisely regulate the industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill gives regulators a broad set of tools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is up to the Government to decide if the industry will be shaped by a hammer or a chisel.
