speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The P2P passenger transport services, including the street-hail and ride-hail services, form an important part of the transport services in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am not sure about other families, but I recall that when I was younger, taking a taxi was a luxury and you would only do so when you really needed to get somewhere fast or had a lot of things to carry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: PHCs were not always accessible to the masses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Now, it is more commonplace to see people using P2P transport services, especially with the entry and proliferation of the PHCs in the sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It, therefore, becomes imperative to have proper rules regulating the sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of my residents are PHC drivers and have shared some challenges they face dealing with competition and with customers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In a conversation with one resident, he shared his concerns about the impact of further rules, especially on penalties that may affect the income he eventually brings home.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have also received feedback calling for parity and fairness to the drivers, in making rules regulating this sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Someone shared that some drivers include extra additional fares to the actual fare without the passenger knowing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is especially the case when the passenger makes the driver wait quite long and the driver arbitrarily charges the passenger for "waiting time".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This does not seem right but some drivers feel that the "waiting penalty" is fair because they say that, very often, passengers will book way in advance and have the drivers wait for them at the passengers' convenience.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, the wait can be up to 15 minutes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Besides lowering their potential income, they may also incur fines if they are waiting in a no-parking area in the Central Business District.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There was also a feedback on the fare start and stop for PHC drivers or the ride-hail services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: An example given by a PHC driver is that a passenger made the driver drive all the way up seven storeys in an industrial park building to reach the exact unit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Because of the large size of the building, it may take close to 10 minutes to reach the top of the building.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is even as the destination was supposed to be arrival foyer of the building itself.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Drivers also said that surge-pricing is a good mechanism as it does encourage drivers to come out and drive when the supply of drivers on the road is low.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Drivers are notified of higher prices and are "activated" and motivated to drive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, some drivers wish to get more clarity on how much of the fare actually goes to the drivers and how much just goes to the companies or operators.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the point is that drivers are asking for some fairness as authorities set rules to regulate conduct with passengers and the business operations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Other points relating to regulations include whether we want to regulate cancellation policies as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am informed that some operators may not charge cancellation charges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are we looking at specific rules to regulate these issues?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On passenger safety, I would like to ask if there is a need to regulate and enforce a certain standard for reporting of emergency situations during rides.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, are there standard operating procedures (SOPs) that the companies adhere to upon receiving the report and whether there is also a need to regulate such SOPs?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The improvements have, indeed, raised convenience and service levels of such transport services in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should encourage continued innovation on this front.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that we do need to strike the balance between regulation and allowing for some space for the sector to grow.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe it is important to continue to share and engage drivers and operators to improve this sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Notwithstanding the inputs I gave above, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the proposed initiatives to level the playing field and make the industry more contestable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both consumers and drivers stand to benefit from more clarity and uniformity in how the rules are applied for street-hail and ride-hail services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the introduction of code of practices across the industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Standardisation is welcomed as it levels the playing field.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While sections 30(2), 30(3) and 30(4) suggest some possible areas that the codes of practice might cover, we do not know how specific or prescriptive the codes will be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that LTA will conduct thorough stakeholder consultation when drafting these codes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important to engage key stakeholders, such as industry partners, in the consultation process to ensure that the codes of practice do not hinder innovation and market forces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, in line with the aim of the Bill to safeguard consumer interest, I hope we can adopt international best practices of having an emergency alarm service button in the vehicle and tracking real-time locations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a feature that is already available for some ride-hail services through the mobile application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, Grab riders are able to request assistance or notify up to three emergency contacts with an in-app Emergency button.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Riders who tap on the button will receive a call from a security company and unanswered calls may be escalated to the Police.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This could be a feature available to both drivers and passengers in the event they face a security threat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also recommend that we require both street-hail and ride-hail services to have child safety seats, as many Members have previously stated as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is currently illegal for private cars, including ride-hail services, to ferry children under 1.35 metres without a child restraint appropriate for the child's height and weight, a booster seat to supplement the seat belt, or an approved adjustable seat belt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Oddly, the street-hail services are exempt from this requirement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This inconsistency in application of the law is not in the interest of the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why should there be a compromise on child safety for street-hail?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From a safety perspective, there should be equal treatment across the board.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, while I agree that it is necessary for PTC to have oversight of prices, it is important not to overreach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill gives PTC the discretion to set a pricing policy for fares charged by ride-hailing operators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the limits to the powers of PTC in relation to ride-hail services?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a move in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an improvement from our current framework that regulates taxi operators, which provide both street-hail and ride-hail services, but handles the ride-hail service sector with a very light touch.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, service delivery standards are largely left to the ride-hail companies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since both taxis and PHCs serve members of the public, I am glad to note that this inconsistency will be rectified with the new legislation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An article titled "Disruption" in this year's 28 January issue of Bloomberg Businessweek described an accident involving a Grab vehicle in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The writer asked, "Was it possible, for all the convenience ride-hailing services offered, they were making cities less safe?" This is a pertinent question.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most PHC drivers work part-time and many are more dependent on GPS assistance compared to taxi drivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even their vehicles may be unfamiliar if they are rented, unlike taxi drivers who also lease, but usually operate the same or a similar vehicle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This combination of factors makes them more vulnerable to traffic accidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Passengers want certain standards, especially for safety, driving competence and route knowledge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new rules are intended to provide greater regulatory oversight for the protection and safety of commuters and drivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Ministry to empower LTA to obtain all the necessary data from all service providers to inform and update its regulations for greater protection of passengers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for PHC drivers, we must ensure that they are in good health and mental condition to drive safely and competently, just as we expect from taxi drivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will provide greater assurance to passengers, many of whom have expressed concerns over dynamic pricing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I agree that there should be leeway to allow fares to fluctuate based on demand, I feel that there should be upper limits set to protect the interests of commuters.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Next, I would like to express my support for the proposal to empower PTC to regulate fares set by ride-hailing operators.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will provide greater assurance to passengers, many of whom have expressed concerns over dynamic pricing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I agree that there should be leeway to allow fares to fluctuate based on demand, I feel there should also be upper limits set to protect the interests of commuters.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, one of the objectives of this Bill is to ensure that we have sufficient regulatory oversight to protect the safety and interests of commuters and drivers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Back in February 2017, I spoke in this House on the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I highlighted how the entry of PHC operators, such as Grab and Uber, has led to a seismic shift in commuter behaviour, as well as many people opting to become freelance PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, while the taxi industry comes under more regulations, there are limited regulations for the PHC P2P passenger transport sector.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Only the drivers and the vehicles come under some form of regulations but the main service providers, such as Grab, which provide the platform, are not regulated.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a sense, this Bill seeks to level the playing field between taxis and PHCs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To apply for a TDVL, one must be at least 30 years old at point of application.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Assuming a person passed his driving test soon after turning 18, a taxi driver would have at least 10 years of driving experience.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, someone applying for a PDVL only needs to have held his driving licence for two years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Assuming the driver takes his driving test soon after turning 18, a PHC driver may not even be 21 years old.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, having obtained a driving licence for more than two years is not the same as having two years of driving experience.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, now we have a situation where we would not trust a 20-year-old to act wisely when voting, but he is trusted to ferry our children and loved ones from P2P in a PHC.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Anecdotally, I see a lot of PHC drivers who drive at excessive speeds and not following basic road manners.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I suppose this might be related to the relatively young age of the drivers as well as lack of maturity.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Older and more experienced drivers who have experienced one or two minor accidents would have learnt to be more patient on the roads.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Existing PHC drivers who are below the age of 25 may continue to drive.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second suggestion is that someone applying for a PDVL must demonstrate that he has owned or rented a car or be a named driver in the car insurance of a family car for at least two years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will level the playing field to bring the rules for PHC closer to those applicable for taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding my comments and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Regulating PHC ride fares will benefit the population at large.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Stipulating the Codes of Practice gives a common framework of standards for the different players in the ride-hail and street-hail services to provide a consistent experience for passengers while ensuring their safety and comfort.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am decidedly pleased that sections 2f and 3f of clause 30 of the Codes of Practice explicitly specify measures to facilitate access to, and use of, the ride-hail and street-hail services by individuals with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, I would like to ride​ on this Bill and the recent announcement of the SG Cares-GoJek Medical Transport Subsidy Scheme in Kembangan-Chai Chee by none other than our dear Speaker himself to discuss how we can push the envelope further for a people, private and public (3P) partnership to support the P2P transportation needs of vulnerable groups in our community as part of our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To support this accessibility, we must also look at how we can train current and potential drivers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Where I was informed is the spread of P2P transport schemes that are currently available for our vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we have the Medical Escort and Transport (MET) services, funded by MOH for community providers to provide transportation and/or someone to accompany their vulnerable clients to travel to and from their homes for medical appointments and treatments, for example, at hospitals, specialist outpatient clinics or polyclinics.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we have the Taxi Subsidy Scheme (TSS) funded by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) which specifically targets people with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The scheme only covers school, work or training supported by SG Enable.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we have the voluntary welfare organisation (VWO) Transport Subsidy Scheme also funded by MSF which, I guess, should be now called SSA Transport Subsidy Scheme since we have now officially dropped the "VWO" for Social Service Agencies (SSAs).

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This scheme supports PWDs who are attending Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children (EIPIC), Day Activity Centres, Sheltered Workshops or Special Education (SPED) schools.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It looks like he would need to apply to one organisation for help to his medical appointment under MET service and another to bring him to day rehab under the VWO transport subsidy scheme.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: From what I understand, only a handful of organisations like HWA and Red Cross can provide a one-stop shop for all these services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the perplexing fragmentation, there is also the unnecessary exclusion of debilitating conditions from the above schemes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Simon, not his real name, in his late 50s, was diagnosed with terminal stage cancer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He needed to go for chemotherapy and subsequently palliative radiotherapy plus several other medical appointments regularly.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Apparently, the MET scheme does not cover trips for chemotherapy, so he was rejected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, the Singapore Cancer Society stepped in to support him.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, a group of volunteers were there to hold his hand and help him navigate through all this.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I also know of people with severe mental health conditions who clearly cannot manage taking the public transport being rejected by these schemes, too.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the fragmentation and accessibility issues, there is also the issue of availability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In his late 70s and living with dementia, Steven, not his real name, was referred to the MET service after his discharge from the hospital because he had lost his mobility.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The service provider took some time to admit him into the service and, even after being accepted as a client, they could not serve him for his post-discharge appointments because they were all fully booked.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The service could not support on short notice but as his condition deteriorated, there were many appointments that he needed to go for urgently.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If you think that the numbers accessing these P2P transport schemes are negligible, I am here to disappoint you with just these two sets of numbers that I managed to find.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) reported that a projected 60% of these clients will need some form of transport.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: HWA provided more than 77,000 trips in financial year (FY) 2017 for rides catered to medical consultations, rehabilitation sessions, recreational activities, ferrying children with disabilities to and from schools.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They do this through Handicare Cab Scheme, a collaboration with ComfortDelGro to provide wheelchair-bound persons a guaranteed cab during rush hour driven by a specially-trained cabby.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: MET services also provide Taxi Subsidy Scheme, amongst others.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We all know how our lives have changed with the ability to just tap for a Grab or GoJek on our phones and knowing that a driver with a car will be at our doorstep in no time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would not this P2P convenience mean even more for vulnerable persons in our midst who are already struggling with the challenges of money, illness and disabilities?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the growing accessibility needs and existing challenges with availability and responsiveness, I would like to urge the Government to consider partnering the private sector, with their existing technology and drivers, to address this challenge at a national level as part of our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even for a lay person like me – although I did invent a technology product in a past life – it seems completely conceivable that there could be a special button on the booking apps visible only to those who are eligible for the subsidy schemes to access the very same underlying booking platform that will ping to hundreds of drivers out there who are trained and available to come to them within minutes or on advanced booking.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some may even be trained to be medical escorts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The financial process is automated and electronic, relieving the community service providers to provide more high value add services to their clients.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On a side note, there is no reason why Meals on Wheels cannot do the same, too, with the food delivery apps.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not so simple as I have described, I understand of course, but it is definitely not impossible.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This can truly be the kind of socially innovative 3P partnership that we want to see more of for a Smart Nation and as a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Improving accessibility will require drivers to be sensitive to the needs of passengers with access needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We could consider tier-pricing according to the carbon emission of the vehicles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This way, passengers could be nudged to consider the ecological footprint of one's transportation choices in their daily commute.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another pricing structure for PHCs could be based on electric, petrol-electric hybrid, compressed natural gas (CNG), bi-fuel (CNG/petrol) vehicles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will not only push passengers and drivers to opt for more environmentally-conscious options, but will also increase the environmental consciousness of our population.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's pledge to reduce greenhouse gases will require the population's recognition of the severity of the climate crisis, in order for various corporate and civil society stakeholders to resolve the issue in unison.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Making our taxis and PHCs more accessible will allow the burden to be shared between the private sector and our SSAs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Those with access needs can choose among different travel options, thereby affording them more convenience and bringing their options closer to the rest of the population because we must change the focus from mobility to accessibility.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, we simply must use every opportunity we have to shape green habits in our people.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instituting carbon emission-based pricing for our P2P passenger transport services further reinforces our commitment to integrate climate change measures into national strategies and policies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Before I go into addressing the specific issues raised by the Members, I would just like to make a few general points.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The P2P sector is very innovative and rapidly evolving.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is already a wide range of services available.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The operators themselves continue to evolve their service provisions and business models on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This has resulted in benefits to commuters, who have many more options, as Members have highlighted repeatedly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have today, PHCs with child seats, wheelchair-friendly services and we have the availability to book taxis with flat fares.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Members have raised a wide range of issues.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For some, like safety, LTA does need to and will step in to regulate and ensure basic standards.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When we intend to do so, LTA has consulted widely, and where there was consensus or where we could engineer a compromise amongst the various tripartite partners and stakeholders, we did.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are some issues which we could not move on for now and which we will continue to work on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will elaborate a little bit on that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is not necessarily desirable to regulate all aspects of the P2P sector.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For some of the issues, like fare caps and the extent to which we have to push environmentally friendly vehicles, there needs to be a role for the market to play as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to get the right balance between what we regulate and what we leave to the industry, ensuring that our regulations are fit for purpose, but commuters benefit and businesses continue to have space to innovate and grow.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our priorities are to make sure that commuters have good, high-quality and safe services; that the interests of drivers are protected in seeking economic opportunities in the space; and thirdly, that the operators are encouraged to innovate and new operators are encouraged to come in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have to look at some of the controls that we have and some of the levers that we have over ensuring that the market encourages new entrants and innovation, that there are protections for the drivers and the commuters, and especially that the structure protects, ultimately, consumers from excessively high charges as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The next thing that we should do is help commuters to make choices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If this is insufficient to achieve the right kind of outcome, we may then have to intervene further.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we hope that by allowing drivers the choice of who to drive for and commuters the choice of which ride to take, this would effectively give us a multi-homing market and achieve some of the outcomes that we want.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There may be more to be done, but we will watch and see.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira also brought up a general point about harmonisation across the street-hail and ride-hail services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We cannot have an entirely harmonised market; otherwise, you would not have differentiation between street-hail and ride-hail services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, the fundamental point is that we still believe that there is a role for street-hail services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are differences in the kind of vehicles that are needed, the training of the drivers for street-hail and safety, and also the operations associated with a fleet of vehicles under one livery, supporting one brand.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Which is really very different from the operations for ride-hail services, which is about the matching of resources and the appropriate algorithms for that supply and demand.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there is a fundamental difference between what we see as a street-hail operator today and ride-hail operator today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are trying to harmonise some of the regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When we look at the regulations for drivers and vehicles, there is already quite a lot of harmony, and we will continue with that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But for the operators, there needs to be a little bit of differentiation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question on private chauffeured services, such as those provided by limousine companies versus electronic applications, both are considered ride-hail services because the key differentiating factor is that there is a matching between a ride and a commuter, and that ride is prebooked for the commuter.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they will fall under the ambit of the ride-hail services and be subject to similar regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee asked about carpooling activities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Carpool operators are also considered ride-hail service operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, they are not operating at the same scale and are operating for a different outcome: ostensibly, an informal way for drivers to give rides to friends and neighbours.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As we collect data and as we examine the market, if those conditions are breached, we will not hesitate to take firm action against the drivers or the operators that have contravened those regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I agree with Mr Ang Wei Neng that innovation is, indeed, important and both street-hail and ride-hail service operators have been innovating and we assume will continue to innovate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are certainly open to the sandboxes for both street-hail and ride-hail services, and the proposed regulatory regime clearly allows for both.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In looking at such sandbox proposals, LTA will study the specific product and use the full scope of legislative instruments and varying regulatory requirements as appropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Codes of Practice were brought up and, indeed, we will consult heavily with industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have a number of fora to do that and I will explain a little bit about that later on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We encourage the operators to participate in the drawing up of the Codes of Practice.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Without spending too much time, clause 30, subsections (2) and (3) of the Bill expand on the different areas that the Codes of Practice could potentially cover.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Several Members spoke about the importance of ensuring safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked about normalised accident rates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is in contrast, I think, to the data that Mr Dennis Tan had said, suggesting an increase, which is "un-normalised".

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The number for PHCs is only slightly higher at six accidents per 10 million km travelled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, when examining the data, we do have to normalise and, once we normalise it, we see that there has not been a significant change.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we do have to ensure that safety remains at top of mind for the drivers and also for the operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we have to have measures for safety at the driver-level, at the vehicle-level and at the operator-level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the driver-level, we have the vocational licence requirements and we have had that in place since 2017.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Drivers are required to have held a driving licence for two years before they can obtain a PDVL, or for one year before they can obtain a TDVL.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing suggested that owning a car or renting a car may be necessary to ensure that drivers are safe.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, just owning or renting a car actually does not necessarily make you any safer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, we have, therefore, not imposed this and we do not have any plans to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked about health screening, which is another way of ensuring driver safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have regular medical check-ups and driving fitness tests for taxi and PHC drivers aged 50 and older.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is more than what is required for private drivers and this is in addition to the mandatory health screening and training requirements at the point at which they obtain their vocational licences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we will continue to monitor this and review our regulations, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The other thing I will point out is that there were some suggestions that younger PHC drivers are more dangerous.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In fact, the data does not support that at all.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no data to suggest specifically that younger PHC drivers are over-represented in the accidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the vehicle-level for safety, we are also making some changes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Taxis will continue to be required to go for six-monthly inspections.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reason for this differentiation is that the annual mileage for PHCs is almost three times that for private cars at about 48,000 km a year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they need to go for more frequent inspections than the private cars.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Taxis then have an even higher average annual mileage of about 130,000 km and so we will retain the requirement that they be inspected every six months.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thirdly, for safety, at the operator-level, I have explained in my opening speech some of the measures.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want to ensure that the responsibility for safety is taken up by the operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This cannot be the responsibility of the driver only.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, part of the operators' responsibilities is to provide data to LTA, to update the safety measures and to encourage their drivers to drive safely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are some suggestions the Members have made, including Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Ang Wei Neng.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To answer Mr Ang Wei Neng's question, we are still reviewing the data requirements for licensed operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will work with the industry to make sure that those are reasonable and useful.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Rahayu Mahzam made some suggestions about emergency buttons on P2P apps and how operators should respond to emergency reports.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Actually, operators are already starting to take the initiative and offer these types of services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a space in which they can compete against one another for the provision of services to commuters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I must say that when we started consultations for this Bill, there was the sense that this was perhaps something that we could move on and was something we wanted to move on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we consulted the public and the stakeholders quite extensively.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The opinions were very divided; and it was not that the opinions were divided for one group of people against the other.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Amongst the general commuting public, the opinion was divided; amongst the operators, the opinion was divided and amongst the drivers, the opinion was divided.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We were trying to, but we have not been able to engineer a compromise in time for this Bill and we thought we would move ahead with these provisions in the Bill today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The matter is alive, we continue the conversation, we will study the matter further.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the reasons why we thought we could move forward with the Bill prior to settling this matter is that there are already the opportunities today for parents to ensure that their children are in child seats.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When they book a PHC, they can indicate that they need child seats.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, one of the considerations was that child seats today are already available and accessible to parents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The argument can be made that it needs to be more widely available, and that has been made by some Members.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The question is, how to make sure that that is something that the industry can carry and the market can support.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to work on this and I hope Members would be able to support us going forward in trying to achieve that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have to be very clear what our regulatory approach is.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some have asked us not to overreach, whereas other people have asked us to impose an upper limit on fares.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira also suggested that we should prevent operators from offering the same service to different customers for different prices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Leon Perera also asked about flat fares.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I wish to point out that today, flat fares are already offered by a number of operators and, again, like some of the other suggestions, we would encourage that this become a differentiating factor, a potential competitive advantage of one operator against another.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Building on what Mr Gan Thiam Poh has suggested, our fare regulations will ensure that there is transparency at the point that the commuter chooses the ride.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This must be made clear to them: what the fare is or that there is going to be a metered fare in the case of a taxi.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The fare levels are an important part of the process to influence the supply and demand for P2P services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many of the advantages and benefits that we have seen over the last few years, and that Members have spoken about, have come about precisely because the fares have been allowed to work as an efficient resource matching mechanism, ensuring that rides can be found during peak hours.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are many forms of services, each requiring different fare levels.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Given the breadth of service offerings and the dynamic nature of these offerings, we think we best leave it to market forces.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That means that, ultimately, potentially, the most important controls would be the choices made by consumers, by commuters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The operators are, indeed, very alive to this, very sensitised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have any doubt about this, one of the operators, Members would know, offers a durian delivery service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have not taken maximum advantage of surge pricing for this because, I suppose, they assume that, if they do, there will be a public outcry about the price of durians at peak season.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The role of the commuter and the consumer in moderating the behaviour of our various operators here would be very, very important.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Ang Wei Neng raised some examples.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are some areas they raised where it would be more appropriate for the operators to take action, including being clear to drivers about commissions charged, handling cancellations by commuters or drivers or even lost-and-found services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Dennis Tan also raised a question about video recordings.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were a few other issues that do not lie directly under the provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But let me just address some of them in terms of how we are thinking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Driver income and welfare: we do not have comparable data for other cities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think Mr Ang Hin Kee made an important point that if we were to intervene in this space, there will be consequences and tradeoffs in respect of some of the other factors, such as the cost of rental, the fares that are available.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would just point out that the average time worked for full-time drivers is about eight hours.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But unfortunately, that is an average and it does not give us the full picture of a very wide range of working hours.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that includes the very occasional work that some of the PHC drivers do.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Someone might choose to do one or the other.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If we try to constrain and constrict either the operator or the driver too much, firstly, it may reduce the attractiveness of this job and people might find it difficult to enter the job, and it may constrain the supply of drivers and may, ultimately, affect prices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we do have to look at that quite carefully.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I think, in general, eight hours, on average, full-time drivers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Mr Ang Wei Neng made several suggestions about who should be eligible to be a PHC driver.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We agree that this is not an area where we need either foreign manpower or any significant excess of manpower.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the other issue of raising the minimum age is not quite an easy decision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no common consensus on what this age should be.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee suggested 30; Mr Yee Chia Hsing suggested 25.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On one hand, raising the minimum age will affect the number of drivers in the P2P market and, in turn, reduce the taxis and rides available to commuters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the other hand, there are not that many drivers who are in this age bracket.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not very clear that we necessarily need to raise the minimum age.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But in general, I think the concerns brought up are valid.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are going to review the size of the driver pool against the needs of the P2P sector and will study the issue of the driver's age carefully.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will certainly consult all the stakeholders before making a considered decision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: PHCs will continue to be bidded in the COE market like private vehicles.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This will allow us to maintain some flexibility in our PHC pool, so that private cars can continue to be converted to PHCs and vice versa.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they should be drawn from the same COE pool.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Anthea Ong spoke passionately on the transport needs of PWDs and vulnerable persons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We agree that our transport sector as a whole does, indeed, have to cater to the needs of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not entirely clear that the taxi and PHC sector alone can meet those needs, especially those with specialised needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, for dedicated transport by VWOs and transport subsidy schemes, we will continue to work closely with our colleagues in MSF and MOH to ensure that all commuters are taken care of.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We agree with Ms Anthea Ong about the importance of making sure that we address the environmental concerns in this sector as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And some of the PHC booking providers and car rental companies have also done the same and committed to making their entire fleet run on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Again, this is another area in which the commuter and the consumer can perhaps assist in asserting some pressure as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I think it is important that we continue to work with the industry to address the environmental concerns of the transport industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Speaking of working with the industry, the role of the operators, the associations and the drivers in this review has been very important.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have contributed their views extensively; they have provided feedback; we have refined our regulations, hopefully to better meet the needs of the commuter and the industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are also lowering call booking Quality of Service (QoS) standards.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All of these will reduce compliance costs for taxi companies and, ultimately, we hope will also benefit the taxi drivers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have institutionalised the way in which we work with the industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have established through LTA a tripartite platform to discuss strategic and regulatory issues for the PHC sector, in addition to the existing one that we have for taxis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is something that Mr Ang Hin Kee himself has called for and has participated very actively in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee will also be happy to know that we will extend the current dispute management system for taxi drivers to include PHC drivers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We hope that this tripartite approach of bringing the partners together can continue, so as to address the issues of benefits for the drivers and vocational licence holders, address the issues of driver welfare, driver income, what is the appropriate role for the industry, and how we can make sure that the regulations look after the drivers as well as look after the commuters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We started with introducing a registration regime for the third-party taxi booking service operators in 2015.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each step of the way, we took calibrated decisions based on the circumstances, taking into account stakeholder and public feedback.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The sector must and does continue to innovate and evolve to meet the needs of commuters and drivers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to monitor the developments in this space and strike a balance between what to regulate and what to leave to the industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The aim is always to ensure that commuters and drivers benefit, and the businesses continue to have the space to innovate and grow.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I hear my colleagues speak about requirements, whether it is for green vehicles, wheelchairs, baby seats, electric vehicles and the likes of it.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: In Japan, they tried this innovation called JPN Taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: They asked everybody what they wanted in a taxi and they designed a taxi for everyone.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: The cost was three times the existing price of existing taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: No commuters wanted to pay for JPN Taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: What I want to urge MOT and LTA to do is that instead of seeking views from everybody and coming up with this wonderful product that nobody wants to pay for, how do we therefore move forward in addressing the needs, ensuring that commuters, drivers and operators are able to calibrate when such innovations and requirements kick in?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Otherwise, we are going to have these requirements and just say, "Maybe the drivers can figure out how to pay for it or the operators can reduce their fees for it".

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: It just does not bring us anywhere to what a proper, appropriate commuting experience and needs for the future will be.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, I thank Mr Ang Hin Kee for that suggestion to not create a taxi that is three times more expensive that nobody wants to pay for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do need to find a way to make sure that all the needs are met.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But not all the needs need to be met in the same way, by the same platform, or by the same service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It does not mean that every single service, every single vehicle has to be exactly the same.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a point where these regulations become inappropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, for example, the taxis are not required to be multi-purpose vehicles (MPVs).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We take that approach, and we do so in partnership with various industry stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We want to ensure that there is enough fluidity to make sure that a variety of services are available to serve everybody’s needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: First, on commuter multi-homing, from time to time, third-party apps do come up and they try to aggregate services across ride-hailing platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: What is the Senior Minister of State’s view if the platform were to take measures to keep their services off these aggregators?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Would he support Codes of Practice that require the platforms to be opened to such third-party aggregators for multi-homing?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: The second point is price discrimination where you charge different people different prices for the same service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: Am I correct in understanding that that would be permitted as an innovation?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have to launch two apps to compare prices, I think that would be okay.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if you cannot fundamentally install the app on your phone because another app is there, it might be a step too far.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think, for now, we want to step back and let this market evolve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As I have said, for the multi-homing space, the mobility-as-a-service space, there is probably a fair number of iterations to go through before we get the right industry model.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we probably do not want to constrain or intervene too much.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are a regular customer for one of the apps, you can apply a discount code, you can apply points that you already have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am a big fan of public consultation and trying to engineer a compromise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But in this case, it really is a safety issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am just wondering whether we should try to compromise when it comes to safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If you are in a private car and your child is not in a car seat, for repeated offence, you could go to jail.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We have such a heavy penalty because of safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am just wondering how does the safety disappear when that same car becomes a taxi.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I recognise my colleague Mr Ang Hin Kee's point about the cost.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If it is $27, and for a car seat, it becomes $60 or $80, of course, any reasonable person would say no.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But in this case, if $2 more could save the life of your child, I am not sure what is holding us back.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, and as I have made quite clear, I agree with Mr Louis Ng on this, and it is my personal stance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One point is that it is not that there is no safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is possible to assure the safety of that child, and that is currently a choice that parents have to assert.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Bring a child seat along into a taxi.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not that it is not possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is whether people choose to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have three children, as I do, of different ages, and each of them needs a different-sized car seat, potentially, it would be impossible for us to take a taxi unless the taxi had three different child seats in it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are a family of five, then you would have to split up into two taxis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if you are an individual adult looking after three children, it would mean that it would then be impossible for you to get into a taxi which only routinely carries one child seat.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And then, what do you do with your other two children?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do feel that there is an opportunity for safety to be secured, as is today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Yes, it could be better and we would like to do more work on it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I would encourage Mr Louis Ng to participate and help us to get this work done.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Could I ride on this opportunity and ask if the Senior Minister of State would, together with the two Senior Minister of States from MOH and MSF, look at starting an inter-agency workgroup or task force to look at the issues that I have mentioned in the fragmentation, availability and accessibility issues for our vulnerable groups?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would say, though, that the nature of this problem and the market, the services that are provided out there is not quite as Ms Anthea Ong had characterised it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There may be five or six, or potentially a lot more providers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there are a number of agencies, offices, whose task it is to help you navigate that space.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Patients or clients should not have to keep working through the fragmentation, as the Member has described.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The other way of thinking about it is, there is a variety of service providers that are working in different niches to address different client needs, different route needs and different demand needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is probably useful that we have an approach like that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is because, today, one of the fundamental problems we have in this space is an inadequate supply of personnel.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will have to work to make sure that that gap is closed as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there is work ongoing and I will work with my colleagues to see what else LTA and MOT could do to help in the transport space.      .
